analysis.one_liner: Forces federal agencies to repeal two existing rules for every costly new rule they issue.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every federal agency, before issuing a new 'major rule' — one with significant economic impact or costs to consumers — to repeal at least two existing rules to offset its cost. An agency could not issue a rule whose cost exceeds the cost of the rules it repealed unless the law itself requires it or the Office of Management and Budget signs off in writing. National security, military, foreign affairs, and internal agency-procedure rules are exempt [S3]. In practice, this is a 'one-in-two-out' deregulation regime: it treats the stock of existing protections as a budget to be spent down whenever agencies want to act. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and later to a subcommittee; no markup, vote, or further action ever occurred before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that face federal regulation — polluters, financial firms, manufacturers, and others — gain if the bill passes, because every costly new consumer, safety, environmental, or antitrust rule would force the rollback of two existing rules, and any rule exceeding the cost of those rollbacks could be blocked at the White House budget office. The bill also gives regulated parties a procedural weapon: agencies must shrink their rulebook on demand rather than judge each protection on its merits.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each agency to repeal at least two rules before issuing any major rule — one with significant economic impact or costs to consumers — to offset its cost [S3].

Bars an agency from issuing a rule that costs more than the rules it repeals unless a statute requires it or the OMB Director approves in writing, giving the budget office a cost veto over regulation [S3].

The definition of 'major rule' covers rules with significant effects on competition, so the regime would reach antitrust and consumer-protection rulemaking as well as safety and environmental rules [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people pay in the form of whatever protections get repealed to make room for new ones: air and water rules, workplace safety standards, financial consumer protections, or competition rules could all be traded away to clear the path for a new rule, regardless of how valuable they are. The public also loses when agencies simply decline to issue important new rules because the repeal quota makes doing so too costly — protection weakens both by rollback and by inaction.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on federal protections

drawbacks.text: The two-for-one quota is arbitrary: it forces agencies to repeal two existing rules of any kind — however valuable — whenever they issue a major rule, so an outdated rule could be sacrificed while a critical one gets repealed to meet the count [S3].

The cost-cap structure treats all rule costs as burdens and all repeal as savings, counting no benefits, so a rule that saves thousands of lives or prevents billions in consumer losses is still treated as pure cost to be offset [S3].

Giving the OMB Director written-veto power over any rule that exceeds the repeal quota centralizes regulatory policy in the White House budget office, an office not accountable the way agencies with public rulemaking processes are [S3].

Similar one-in-two-out regimes have been criticized by across the political spectrum as hindering necessary regulation during emergencies and weakening long-standing protections; the bill only exempts military, national security, foreign affairs, and internal-agency rules, leaving consumer, health, and financial protections exposed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to regulated industries, which would gain a structural brake on new federal rules and a mechanism to force the retirement of existing ones. The cost falls on the public: fewer and weaker protections against pollution, unsafe products, financial misconduct, and anticompetitive behavior, decided not by evidence but by an arbitrary arithmetic of two-for-one. The bill offers no process for judging whether a repealed rule was redundant or essential, which is the core of the design problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee — first at the House Judiciary Committee, then at a subcommittee — and never got a markup, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. C. Scott Franklin introduced the bill on June 22, 2021, with 12 Republican cosponsors; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1].
On November 1, 2022 — more than 16 months after introduction — it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
No committee markup, committee vote, floor debate, or roll-call vote on the bill occurred at any point in the 117th Congress, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people come out ahead, in the sense that no existing federal protections had to be repealed under the bill's two-for-one quota and agencies faced no cost-cap veto. The failure to advance the bill also spared agencies the structural constraint, while regulated industries did not get the deregulation brake they would have gained if it had passed.

for.name: Rep. C. Scott Franklin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring agencies to repeal two rules before issuing each major rule [S1].

for.name: 12 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, including Reps. Cawthorn, Johnson of Ohio, Salazar, Jackson, Gosar, Moore of Alabama, Greene of Georgia, Biggs, Perry, and Herrell [S3, S4].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill in 18 months; the only action was a referral to a subcommittee on November 1, 2022, which carried no deadline or requirement of action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill received no Democratic support in the record; no votes occurred, so no roll-call split exists [S4].

industries.industry: Regulated industries generally (polluters, manufacturers, financial firms)
industries.note: The bill would give any industry facing a costly new rule a structural shield: agencies would have to repeal two existing rules to issue it, and a cost cap plus OMB approval could block the rule entirely. The industry's gain — fewer and weaker federal rules — comes directly at the expense of the public protections those rules provide.

The CRS summary notes the bill's definition of major rule includes rules with significant adverse effects on competition, so agencies writing competition or consumer-affairs rules would fall under the repeal quota, making antitrust rulemaking harder to pursue [S2].
